title: Godot, Unity, Unreal, something else
author: Livid_Shallot5701
selftext:
Hi,

I made all my games in godot and it seems like ai agents (i use cursor) can use godot realy well. it could literally do anything in my game at any point. i dont say it all looked stunning or it didnt do any errors (lol quite the opposite) BUT it could touch and change everything.

now i am at a point where i want to make a game with 400+ units simultanously and beautiful 3d grafics and i get recommended unreal a lot. BUT i also get told that the influence a coding agent has on unreal is smallöer than on godot.

But i liked that it could solve all problems in godot itself and i was just the author, not the laborer. Now when i switch to unreal i fear that all the manial tasks i could outsource on godot are comming back to me again.

so my question:

to anyone who uses unreal or even better uses both unreal, godot, maybe unity and maybe something else entirely: how much can agents do in each engine and do you realy feel the limitations? or are they so minor that its basically "doesnt matter"?

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body:
godot is easier for llms because of how the files are saved, I don't know about unreal, but pre mcp servers llms had trouble with unity because alot needed to be done in the ui. now that both have cli and mcp support I've seen some decent games. I'm making my own engine, which takes time, this is after 2 weeks of pretty much non stop work  This was all done with just claude code, blender, and some other genertive local models like trellis. Almost everything is procedural either in game, or at least created by opus using blender . the benefit of a 100% custom engine is the agent can just look at the code and change it as needed

https://reddit.com/link/pdokvrb/video/b1m4w0xsdbth1/player

comments.author: EliasWick
comments.body:
Well Unreal is free, so go try it. Although, you can't make a good game with AI. You need to know a lot of coding and workflows for it to make sense.

Godot is a very bare bones engine, Unreal is not and has a bunch if niche things to consider as a developer. Try as best as you can with your AI or agents, it will not take you far without sitting down and actually learning proper game development, design, etc.

replies.author: Livid_Shallot5701
replies.body:
i dont understand your point, i am a designer by heart. but i have no clue about architecture. thats why i use coding agents. 

so i dont realy get what you are getting at and it just sounds like you want to hate on ai use.

replies.author: EliasWick
replies.body: I am saying that if you wont learn the architecture (which will take years), then you might as well pick something else, instead of Unreal. Relying on AI to make your game isn't going to work long term.

replies.body: why wouldnt it, i already made 2 games with it and they worked out just fine. 20 hours average playtime with a price of 10-20€ and one sold 1000 times, the other one 500 times, i am quite happy. but the next one i wanna  aurafarm on ridiculously pleasing aesthetics to go into the 10k copies sold ranks

replies.author: EliasWick
replies.body:
Well, I respect it! Anyways, download Unreal and try. I doubt you'll be happy... it's hard and difficult to make a game there. Eventually with AI, you'll have to spend a few years on it.

For context I am talking about a 2 - 4 hour game with a story, no multiplayer + good graphics, animation and sound.

replies.author: Livid_Shallot5701
replies.body: yes the results from my last 2 hours all point into the direction of "better not use unreal unless i have a few spare years". thanks

replies.author: zenmatrix83
replies.body: the more you know the more likely you will have sucess. Even still with current coding agents, llms still get lost, and will spend many cycles finding missing work. its why people will mention code base sizes, there are techniques that can mitigate issues but an ai only knows what it can fit it its context about your game, not to mention all the other things like tool call history and chat history, [agent.md](http://agent.md) or [claude.md](http://claude.md) files and anything else.

replies.author: EliasWick
replies.body: Definitely! There are some truth to what you are saying. The main issue is context. AI will not in many years be able to keep context of a proper Unreal Engine project. It's too much and too big.

You can still get really beautiful graphics out of unity it just doesn’t have as many tool sets. I’m sure even sota model ais would get a headache trying to unravel performance optimizations on unreal though

comments.author: Spudly42
comments.body:
Unity has good documentation and lots of learnings spread across forums and whatnot, which means LLMs know how to work with it well.  That doesn't apply nearly as well to Unreal and Unreal also has a lot of visual scripting that isn't easy for LLMs.

But if you want it to look nice, the best thing you can really do there is use something with good 3rd party assets that you can buy.  If I had something specific in mind, I'd first start by shopping through the marketplaces of each to see which had the best options for the game I want.

I use Unity with Claude and the pipeline package: [https://docs.unity.com/en-us/unity-cli/unity-pipeline/unity-pipeline-package](https://docs.unity.com/en-us/unity-cli/unity-pipeline/unity-pipeline-package)

You can do pretty much everything, I use it to make Claude play test my game for bugs fixes and to do tedious tasks.

I just had Claude place all my roads tiles for my city instead of manually placing my corners, crossing, straight, pedestrians crossing etc.

It toke 5 minutes to place 250 pieces of road.

comments.author: dreadpirater
comments.body:
I use Codex with Unity regularly.   

It can do ANYTHING in Unity that I know how to do in Unity.    
  
That's careful wording.   I would expect that to hold up in Unreal, too.  If you know HOW to use it, you'll have no trouble prompting something.  If you were hoping it would learn Unreal so you don't have to...That's okay on pretty simple games but as the game gets more complex, yes, you're going to run into a lot of situations where it makes short sighted decisions and you think something's done then come back and find out 'oh, that new system you asked for only works for NPCs named Bob, because you told me to make Bob be able to do it, and now you find out that your cpu will melt when you try to extend the behavior to every NPC...   

That's where a lot of my worry for you is - a lot of what AI knows about game dev it got from reading and watching tutorials... and a lot of tutorials take shortcuts to get to the interesting stuff... which is fine when you're learning but if you don't know to constantly remind the AI of what scale you're headed for, it will continue to deprioritize performant over expedient now.

My strong suggestion for you - learn it along side your agent.  That's actually what I did to get back into Unity recently after years away from it.   "Hey, I want you to create a tutorial series to make this kind of game :  DESCRIBE YOUR GAME.   I want to LEARN as we do it.  I want each lesson to cover one concrete step.  I want you to explain the whole step to me when we enter the step- both high level concepts and concrete application steps - where to find tools that aren't already visible, etc.   At the end of the explanation, ask me what I want to implement and what I want you to implement.   We can build placeholder systems early on, but the goal is to take the tutorial all the way through production, so when we do kludge something, we need to clearly mark that and make it a future tutorial step to revisit and refactor."   

The 'tell me what I need to know about this' step is  two-fold important - it tells YOU what it's doing so you learn, and also, it's forcing a full planning turn before the agent tears into your codebase each time, so it's clear on what to do even if you end every explanation with "You know what, you handle this.   Poke me if there's anything you can't do from the commandline or via the provided tools."  

You can tell it to break it into 60 lessons to be done over 60 days.  You don't have to keep to that timeline but it can be a very good way to get a 'human readable roadmap' since a non-coder's eyes can go crossey staring at a build spec that's written like a build spec.  Having it write it like a tutorial gets it to you in ELI5.
